title: Beverly's Secret

jokes.text: Hank insists on bringing show clothes, a trunk, and avocados for a one-week TV bit living with a Wisconsin family.
jokes.setup: Someone is telling Hank he's overpacking for a week-long TV segment in Wisconsin.
jokes.punchline: Artie: 'Oh, for God's sakes, Hank, you're not goin' off to college, you know. You're spending a week with a family in Wisconsin.'
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank self-importance played against Artie's world-weary pragmatism. The avocados are the perfect absurd specific detail. Strongly character-integrated — Hank's Hollywood grandiosity colliding with a mundane Midwest assignment is the engine of the whole bit.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're not goin' off to college, you know. You're spending a week with a family in wisconsin. Jeez, it's just a bit.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Hank, Charlie's no longer with us.' Hank: 'I know, that's what I'm saying. It's wide open.'
jokes.setup: Artie points out Charles Kuralt has died
jokes.punchline: Hank's response reveals he already knew and sees Kuralt's death purely as a market opportunity
jokes.explanation: This is a crisp, compact exchange that earns its darkness. Hank's moral vacuum is laid bare — a dead icon becomes nothing more than a cleared lane. The economy is exceptional: 'I know, that's what I'm saying. It's wide open' does everything in nine words. Character-specific to Hank's oblivious self-absorption. One of the tightest jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Why should Charles kuralt have a monopoly on this kind of shit?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank, Charlie's no longer with us.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I know, that's what I'm saying. It's... it's wide open.

jokes.text: Hank's 'bit with enormous spin-off potential' — comparing himself to Charles Kuralt, who is dead.
jokes.setup: Hank defends the Wisconsin family bit by citing its 'enormous spin-off potential' and invoking Charles Kuralt.
jokes.punchline: Artie: 'Hank, Charlie's no longer with us.' Hank: 'I know, that's what I'm saying. It's wide open.'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. Hank's logic — that Kuralt's death is an *opportunity* for him — is perfectly monstrous and specific to Hank's narcissism. The structure is airtight: Artie delivers the gentle corrective, Hank pivots to crass opportunism without missing a beat. The 'wide open' punchline lands with real impact because it reveals how Hank processes the world.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just realized when I said steven wright, you were actually to my right. It's a good thing your name isn't steven left because I'd be looking this way.

jokes.text: Larry to Steven Wright: 'I just realized when I said Steven Wright, you were actually to my right. It's a good thing your name isn't Steven Left because I'd be looking this way.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing small-talk on the talk show couch with comedian Steven Wright.
jokes.punchline: Larry points out the directional coincidence of Wright's name, then extends it to the absurd 'Steven Left' hypothetical.
jokes.explanation: A serviceable wordplay joke but the kind of thin, filler banter late-night hosts actually do. It works as verisimilitude — Larry trying too hard with a comedian who's notoriously flat — but the joke itself is weak. The extension to 'Steven Left' is the only save.

dialogue.speaker: Steven Wright
dialogue.line: Stephen hawking was mad at me 'cause I took his parking space, and... I said to him, 'don't you have better things to think about?'

jokes.text: Steven Wright: 'Stephen Hawking was mad at me 'cause I took his parking space, and I said to him, "Don't you have better things to think about?"'
jokes.setup: Wright mentions attending a benefit at the planetarium where Stephen Hawking was present.
jokes.punchline: He stole Hawking's parking space (implying a handicapped space) and told the world's greatest theoretical physicist not to worry about it.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed Wright-style joke delivered in-character on the show's fictional talk show. The layered offensiveness (parking space implication + dismissing Hawking's intellect) is perfectly calibrated. 'Don't you have better things to think about?' is quotable and lands with authority. Works as both a Steven Wright bit AND as the show using a real comedian naturally.

dialogue.speaker: Steven Wright
dialogue.line: I go to lots of the games, uh-huh. I follow the team regularly, yeah. I love going to fenway park... I do not consider myself a fan. I don't want to be labeled.

jokes.text: Steven Wright on being a Red Sox fan: 'I go to lots of the games. I follow the team regularly. I love going to Fenway Park... I do not consider myself a fan. I don't want to be labeled.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Wright is a Red Sox fan — clearly a yes/no question.
jokes.punchline: Wright enumerates every behavior of fandom then refuses the label, citing aversion to being labeled.
jokes.explanation: A tight comedic structure — the escalating list of fan behaviors building to an absurd denial of the obvious conclusion. Wright's deadpan commitment to anti-labeling irrationalism is perfectly in character for his comedic persona. The joke earns its laughs through structure and the delightful logic of the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Steven Wright
dialogue.line: I've been studying Italian for years because I have to study it 'cause I eventually want to teach it.

jokes.text: Steven Wright says he's studying Italian so he can eventually teach it — implying years of study are just preparation to teach, not to speak.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Wright has learned a foreign language. Wright says he's been studying Italian for years.
jokes.punchline: 'I've been studying Italian for years because I have to study it 'cause I eventually want to teach it.'
jokes.explanation: A quietly funny Wright-ism: the recursive absurdity of studying to teach rather than to use the skill. The circular logic is classic Wright and works in the show's context as an interview answer that goes nowhere productive.

dialogue.speaker: Steven Wright
dialogue.line: I've been raising horses for years. They're getting taller and taller, and, um, it's goin' great. You should come over sometime. We'll watch them.

jokes.text: Steven Wright on raising horses: 'They're getting taller and taller, and it's going great. You should come over sometime. We'll watch them.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Wright is raising horses. Wright enthusiastically confirms.
jokes.punchline: The payoff to 'raising horses' is that they are 'getting taller and taller' — the most banal possible observation about growth — and the invitation to 'watch them.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: the anticlimactic observation that horses grow taller (which is what all horses do), delivered as a proud achievement, and then the absurd intimacy of 'come over, we'll watch them.' Perfect Wright energy — understated enthusiasm for nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Steven Wright
dialogue.line: Horses are a fabulously interesting animal. They're one of the only species named that.

jokes.text: Steven Wright: 'Horses are a fabulously interesting animal. They're one of the only species named that.'
jokes.setup: The conversation continues about horses.
jokes.punchline: 'They're one of the only species named that.' — i.e., named 'horses,' which is tautologically true of every species.
jokes.explanation: This is the best Wright joke in the episode and one of the sharper gags in the transcript. The joke sounds like it's building to a factoid but the punchline is a tautology dressed as insight — every species is 'one of the only species named that.' The genius is that it takes a moment to unpack, which is the Wright signature. Perfect economy, highly quotable, and only Wright (or this show's version of Wright) could deliver it.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Lou
dialogue.line: I did that once. I lost 15 pounds, but I gained it all back.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I'm not bulimic.

jokes.text: Larry, coming off stage, immediately asks where Beverly is — the show still happening in background is irrelevant to him.
jokes.setup: The on-air segment with Wright just ended ('very, very funny, both of you').
jokes.punchline: Larry's first post-segment concern is not the show but Beverly's whereabouts — a small reveal of his self-absorption and office-world priorities.
jokes.explanation: A subtle Larry character beat — the show is secondary to his interpersonal anxieties. Works as character texture more than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant, all right?

dialogue.speaker: Mary Lou
dialogue.line: Oh, my God. Congratulations. Who's the father?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I don't want to discuss it.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Lou
dialogue.line: It's not Larry, is it?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Close?

jokes.text: Mary Lou's first question after learning Beverly is pregnant: 'Who's the father?' Her second: 'It's not Larry, is it?'
jokes.setup: Beverly reveals she is pregnant and doesn't want to discuss the father.
jokes.punchline: Mary Lou immediately asks if it's Larry — the workplace-gossip escalation is both believable and funny, and the paranoid possibility that it might be is treated as real.
jokes.explanation: The rapid escalation from 'who?' to 'is it Larry?' in one beat is efficient comedy writing. The Larry possibility is immediately plausible given the show's dynamics, which makes it funnier. Beverly's non-denial ('Close?') adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Lou
dialogue.line: I keep thinking it's Martin lawrence.

dialogue.speaker: Other Writer
dialogue.line: Naw, he's too wild. His idea of a first date is driving into a tree.

jokes.text: Beverly says the father was 'a guest' and won't say who. Mary Lou/colleague: 'Keep thinking it's Martin Lawrence.' Response: 'Naw, he's too wild. His idea of a first date is driving into a tree.'
jokes.setup: The staff learns Beverly's baby's father was a show guest and begin speculating.
jokes.punchline: Martin Lawrence is ruled out because 'his idea of a first date is driving into a tree' — a reference to Lawrence's real-life incident of running his car into a telephone pole while armed.
jokes.explanation: A sharp insider joke using a real celebrity scandal as a punchline. 'His idea of a first date is driving into a tree' is nicely economical and dark. The joke works better in its original broadcast era but holds up as a time-capsule dark gag.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: I know things you guys don't want to know about Richard mulligan.

jokes.text: 'Oh, no, Beverly likes wild men. I know things you guys don't want to know about Richard Mulligan.'
jokes.setup: Colleagues are speculating about Beverly's taste in men.
jokes.punchline: The invocation of Richard Mulligan (a relatively obscure TV actor) as a 'wild man' with implied scandalous behavior is absurdly specific and funny precisely because he's not a name you'd expect.
jokes.explanation: The joke's originality comes from the unexpected name drop — Richard Mulligan instead of an obvious celebrity. The 'things you don't want to know' withholding makes it funnier than an explicit punchline would. Insider showbiz flavor.

dialogue.line: Oh, yeah! Yeah, because he's tired of fucking Claudia schiffer.

jokes.text: Staff betting pool on who fathered Beverly's baby — 'the potato chip lady,' 'the log man,' David Copperfield ('he's tired of fucking Claudia Schiffer').
jokes.setup: The staff, having learned Beverly's baby's father is a show guest, immediately turns it into a betting pool.
jokes.punchline: The candidates escalate absurdly — 'potato chip lady,' 'log man,' then David Copperfield with the brutal aside about Claudia Schiffer.
jokes.explanation: The betting pool device is a great structural move — it transforms the pregnancy into absurdist comedy while also skewering late-night TV's guest ecosystem. 'He's tired of fucking Claudia Schiffer' is the sharpest line in the sequence, unexpectedly direct and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: I just want to make a straight bet, 50 bucks, Billy dee Williams.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: Oh, that is so 1970s.

jokes.text: Artie delivers the note that 'beloved Larry' wants another pass on the Richard Simmons space shuttle skit. When asked what's wrong with it, Artie: 'I believe the word "bad" was bandied about.'
jokes.setup: Artie delivers Larry's note about rewriting a sketch.
jokes.punchline: 'I believe the word "bad" was bandied about' — Artie's magnificently understated way of saying the sketch is terrible.
jokes.explanation: Peak Artie — magnificent economy and understatement. 'Bandied about' is a perfectly chosen formal phrase to deliver devastating criticism. This is exactly the kind of line Rip Torn could deliver like a blade. The 'beloved Larry' setup (passive-aggressive formality from a boss) adds another layer.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I believe the word 'bad' was bandied about.

jokes.text: Artie discovers the office betting pool on Beverly's pregnancy and says 'Show some decency. This is Beverly.' — then immediately asks 'Jimmy Caan? No way. He's still tied up in court.'
jokes.setup: Artie catches the staff running a betting pool on who fathered Beverly's baby, scolds them for decency.
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately participates by dismissing Jimmy Caan as a candidate — 'He's still tied up in court' — revealing his hypocrisy.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best constructed jokes in the episode. The setup — Artie's righteous scolding — is played completely straight, making the instant pivot to 'Jimmy Caan? He's still tied up in court' both a shock and a perfect character revelation. It's Artie's hypocrisy made funny, and 'still tied up in court' is a great dark specific detail. The speed of the turn is what elevates it.

dialogue.line: Jimmy caan?
No way. He's still tied up in court.

jokes.text: 'Jimmy Caan? No way. He's still tied up in court.'
jokes.setup: Someone nominates Jimmy Caan as the father
jokes.punchline: Artie rules him out not on moral grounds but because his legal troubles would interfere with fatherhood duties
jokes.explanation: This is the punchline that makes joke 18 work as a full unit. On its own it's a sharp celebrity-shade line with good economy. As the callback to Artie's fake moral outrage, it's elevated significantly. The use of 'still tied up in court' as a practical disqualifier rather than a moral one is the key insight.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A lot of people don't know Hank used to work at the house of pies before he worked here.

jokes.text: Live cut to Hank in Wisconsin making apple pie; Larry tells viewers: 'A lot of people don't know Hank used to work at the House of Pies before he worked here.'
jokes.setup: Larry introduces the Wisconsin segment where Hank is baking
jokes.punchline: The throwaway revelation that Hank's pre-fame career was at House of Pies — pathetic backstory delivered as charming anecdote
jokes.explanation: Works as background character color — House of Pies is such a specific, unglamorous detail that it quietly undercuts Hank's pretensions. The joke is soft but consistent with the episode's sustained Hank-degradation.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: she was the, uh, first one, uh, in her neighborhood to own a minsk coat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I think he means 'mink.'

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, she was from minsk.

jokes.text: Hank: 'She was the first one in her neighborhood to own a minsk coat.' Larry: 'I think he means mink.' Hank: 'No, she was from Minsk.'
jokes.setup: Hank is telling the story of his Russian grandmother's coat.
jokes.punchline: Hank conflates 'mink' (fur coat) with 'Minsk' (the city), and when corrected insists he meant the city — he genuinely doesn't see the confusion.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly executed Hank stupidity joke. The wordplay is simple but the structure is excellent — the correction and Hank's oblivious counter-correction ('No, she was from Minsk') is the move that makes it land. Hank doesn't realize he's done anything wrong, which is the character's tragic comedy in a nutshell.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank, I'm no expert on pies, but that one looks like it needs to go back in for another 3 or 4 hours.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You forgot to turn the oven on.

jokes.text: Hank's 'ahead-of-time' baking reveal: he pulls out a raw/underbaked pie. Larry: 'That one looks like it needs to go back in for another 3 or 4 hours. You forgot to turn the oven on.'
jokes.setup: Hank brags he 'thought ahead' and pre-baked a pie so they could see the finished product on air.
jokes.punchline: The pie is clearly raw/underbaked because Hank forgot to turn the oven on — a classic 'thought ahead but failed basic step' comedy structure.
jokes.explanation: A visual gag inferred from dialogue — the pie is clearly terrible. Hank's self-congratulatory setup ('I thought ahead') makes the failure funnier. A reliable sitcom structure executed with good timing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Why don't you put your head in there, Hank? See if it's working.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Why don't you put your head in there, Hank? See if it's working.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just told Hank the pie looks underbaked and the oven wasn't turned on.
jokes.punchline: Larry's casual suggestion that Hank put his head in the oven — simultaneously a practical suggestion and a death wish — delivered completely deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Dark, efficient, and perfectly in character for Larry's passive-aggressive relationship with Hank. The double meaning (check the oven / stick your head in the oven) is left implicit, which is the right call. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm turning into bud melman.

jokes.text: Larry, offstage after a bad show segment: 'I'm turning into Bud Melman.'
jokes.setup: The Hank Wisconsin bit has been going terribly; Larry is frustrated post-taping.
jokes.punchline: Larry compares himself to Calvert DeForest (Bud Melman), David Letterman's famously awkward recurring bit player — a devastating self-comparison for a talk-show host.
jokes.explanation: An insider-comedy reference that works on multiple levels: Larry's wounded pride, the specific fear of becoming a supporting-cast comedy prop, and the meta-showbiz awareness of the comparison. Beautifully economical — four words that say everything.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: not a bunch of yokels make Hank look like... an asshole!

jokes.text: Larry's correction of the Wisconsin bit's premise: 'The premise is Hank moves in with a bunch of yokels, not a bunch of yokels make Hank look like... an asshole!'
jokes.setup: Larry is post-show, furious about how the Hank Wisconsin segment went.
jokes.punchline: The pause before 'an asshole' — and the word itself — lands as both the critique and the inadvertent truth about the whole bit.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Larry's furious defense of a premise that is itself premised on condescension toward 'yokels.' The pause before 'asshole' is the structural moment — the audience knows the word is coming but the delivery matters. Larry's anger is the real joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Tonight, didn't it seem more like 54 minutes?

jokes.text: Larry's sign-off: 'Anyway, thanks for being here tonight. I know it went quickly. I can't believe this is an hour-long talk show myself. Tonight, didn't it seem more like 54 minutes?'
jokes.setup: Larry closes the show after a rough night.
jokes.punchline: 'Tonight, didn't it seem more like 54 minutes?' — a sardonic acknowledgment that the show felt short, possibly because so much went wrong.
jokes.explanation: A dry Larry sign-off joke — meta-awareness about the show's quality dressed as a runtime observation. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: lady luck just gave me a blow job.

jokes.text: Larry, privately: 'Who can sleep? I won't be able to sleep.' — implying genuine distress about the bad show segment.
jokes.setup: Larry just told the audience to 'sleep well.'
jokes.punchline: The moment the cameras are off, Larry admits he can't sleep — his public ease is a complete performance.
jokes.explanation: A characteristic Larry beat — the gap between his on-air persona and his off-air anxious reality. Works as character comedy more than a laugh-out-loud joke.

dialogue.line: He was drinking again. He was doing so well. 91 days.

jokes.text: Off-camera chaos: someone wins big at what sounds like poker ('3 queens') and yells 'lady luck just gave me a blow job.' Another voice: 'Shh! Everybody calm down. We didn't hear a thing.'
jokes.setup: Post-show, some kind of off-screen commotion erupts backstage.
jokes.punchline: 'Lady luck just gave me a blow job' — crudely delivered then immediately covered up by the 'we didn't hear a thing' reaction.
jokes.explanation: A raw, backstage moment of vulgar exuberance — contextually funny as a behind-the-scenes tone shift but not a crafted joke. The cover-up reaction adds a small beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Maybe you should come in a few minutes early each morning, and then you could make some protein shakes, and then, you know, there they'd be.

jokes.text: Someone backstage: 'He was drinking again. He was doing so well. 91 days.'
jokes.setup: Post-poker chaos backstage, someone apparently drinking.
jokes.punchline: The precision of '91 days' — someone has been counting — delivered matter-of-factly as a backstage aside, treating a relapse as a minor workplace inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '91 days' is what makes it darkly funny — someone was tracking, and it's all for nothing. Typical Larry Sanders Show treatment of serious issues as texture rather than drama.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: If you think I'm gonna come in even a minute early, I think you're out of your mind, because I have a life, OK?

jokes.text: A woman (wife/girlfriend of the person drinking): 'He's not the man I married.' — delivered as emotional distress in a backstage corridor during a late-night talk show.
jokes.setup: The backstage chaos of a relapse; someone comforting a distraught woman.
jokes.punchline: The incongruity of this soap-opera melodrama happening in the backstage of a talk show, delivered completely sincerely.
jokes.explanation: More tone/texture than crafted joke — the show uses this kind of background chaos as world-building. The comedy is contextual (talk show backstage as soap opera) rather than intrinsic.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What the fuck was that about?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Larry, she's pregnant.

jokes.text: Larry wanders into the kitchen looking for a protein shake, finds Beverly in a private moment. He suggests she come in earlier (or stay later) to make protein shakes pre-emptively. Beverly: 'Larry, I'm in this office already for 12 hours. If you think I'm gonna come in even a minute early, I think you're out of your mind, because I have a life, OK?'
jokes.setup: Larry stumbles in looking for a protein shake, interrupts Beverly, and immediately pivots to making her job harder.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's explosion — '12 hours... I have a life' — delivered to a boss who is clearly oblivious to basic human consideration.
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders cringe: Larry's solipsism at its most nakedly absurd — he's literally interrupting a private moment to request a protein shake, then doubles down by asking her to work longer hours. Beverly's outburst is earned. The comedy is in Larry's complete blindness to his own behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, why didn't, um... she tell me?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, we thought she should, but she didn't, 'cause, you know, she didn't want to hurt your feelings. You know how close you two are.

jokes.text: Larry learns Beverly is pregnant. His first question: 'Well, why didn't she tell me?' Then: 'Is she married? Is she dating someone? Well, who is it?'
jokes.setup: Staff tells Larry that Beverly is pregnant and didn't tell him to spare his feelings.
jokes.punchline: Larry's reaction is entirely about his own feelings and his desire to know gossip — not concern for Beverly.
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective character moment — Larry's instinctive narcissism revealed through the sequence of his questions. He never asks if Beverly is okay.

dialogue.speaker: Eriq La Salle
dialogue.line: You think I should leave E.R?

jokes.text: Larry is told the father is 'one of tonight's guests.' He runs through the list: 'Drew Carey, Eriq La Salle, Michael Bolton?' — then immediately goes to warmly greet Eriq La Salle.
jokes.setup: Larry just learned Beverly's baby's father is one of that night's guests.
jokes.punchline: Larry cycles through the suspects, then walks directly into the most awkward possible greeting with Eriq La Salle — the interaction is loaded with double meaning the audience understands.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully awkward structural setup — Larry's hyper-solicitous greeting to La Salle ('Is everything all right? Need anything?') is now read by the audience as either suspicion or obsequiousness. The dramatic irony is thick and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Schmidt
dialogue.line: I said, when I got back, I wanted you gone.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: All right.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Schmidt
dialogue.line: Did you hear me?

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Schmidt
dialogue.line: I want him out of here now. He can take his whore with him, OK?

jokes.text: Larry tells Eriq La Salle: 'Whenever I've had a problem, I always tried to do the thing I'm most afraid of.' La Salle: 'You think I should leave E.R.?'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to give oblique advice, seemingly about Beverly's situation, to Eriq La Salle.
jokes.punchline: La Salle completely misreads the advice as being about his TV career, not his personal life — and it's a reasonable misread.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection — Larry's vague advice (deliberately oblique because he doesn't know the situation) gets misread as career advice. La Salle's 'You think I should leave E.R.?' is a perfect punchline because it's both absurd and completely logical given the ambiguity.

dialogue.speaker: Drew Carey
dialogue.line: Listen to your body. Gimme a porno tape and a pizza.
Ah, comin' right up.

dialogue.speaker: Drew Carey
dialogue.line: Yes, o best body, I obey.

jokes.text: During the Wisconsin bit, Hank is holding a feather duster. Larry: 'Oh, that's a relief.' — then: 'When you win a week with Hank, you get a full range of services.'
jokes.setup: Hank is shown on location holding a feather duster in the Schmidt family home.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'that's a relief' implies what else a feather duster might suggest in Hank's hands. Then 'full range of services' doubles down on the innuendo.
jokes.explanation: Light innuendo, well-executed. 'That's a relief' is the better of the two lines — the implication is funnier than the explicit follow-up.

dialogue.speaker: Drew Carey
dialogue.line: Chef boyardee, aunt jemima, fightin' Irish. / 'Cause all I can tell you, if you're an American indian, and you're offended by the logo, all I can tell you is, hey, you should have fought harder.

jokes.text: The Schmidt husband interrupts the bit: 'I said, when I got back, I wanted you gone. Did you hear me? I want him out of here now. He can take his whore with him.' — while Larry narrates the segment as if everything is fine.
jokes.setup: Hank is performing the 'week with a family' bit while the actual family dynamic is clearly in crisis.
jokes.punchline: An actual domestic confrontation ('He can take his whore with him') explodes in the background while Larry narrates pleasantries ('Looks like a delightful place the Schmidts have').
jokes.explanation: A brilliant cringe-comedy set piece: the wholesome 'America's family' bit is invaded by an actual domestic implosion, and Larry keeps narrating as if it isn't happening. The juxtaposition of 'He can take his whore with him' and 'Looks like a delightful place the Schmidts have' is the joke, and it's perfectly timed. This is the Wisconsin bit paying off its setup with maximum darkness.

dialogue.line: If women ran the country, there would be no war.
Yeah, I'm sure no one would start a fight for no reason at all if women ran the world.

jokes.text: After the Schmidt meltdown, Artie quietly: 'I can't find any of this on the page.'
jokes.setup: Domestic chaos just erupted live on the Wisconsin bit.
jokes.punchline: Artie's dry acknowledgment that none of the domestic meltdown was in the script — treating a crisis as a production logistics problem.
jokes.explanation: Artie's reaction beat is executed with perfect economy. 'I can't find any of this on the page' is the ideal response to chaos — bureaucratic, unruffled, absurd. It's Rip Torn's deadpan at its finest, and the economy (one line, nine words) is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Drew Carey
dialogue.line: You mention one hooker, you gotta mention 'em all. You never think they could be so territorial, but Jesus Christ.

jokes.text: Drew Carey on joining the Warner Bros. gym: trainer tells him to 'listen to your body.' Carey: 'How do you think my body got like this in the first place? Listen to your body. Gimme a porno tape and a pizza.'
jokes.setup: Drew Carey describes joining a gym and being told to 'listen to your body.'
jokes.punchline: 'How do you think my body got like this in the first place?' — his body's instructions are for porno tapes and pizza, not fitness.
jokes.explanation: A tight Carey-brand self-deprecating joke with strong structure. The 'listen to your body' premise is the setup, and the pivot to what his body actually wants ('porno tape and pizza') is funny and specific to his persona. Well-executed and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Drew Carey
dialogue.line: Great to be here at caesars. I've only been here a day. I'm already up 10 grand. Of course, I had to let a fat arab fuck me up the ass, but, hey.

jokes.text: Drew Carey on the Cleveland Indians logo controversy: 'All I can tell you, if you're an American Indian and you're offended by the logo, all I can tell you is, hey, you should have fought harder.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Carey discuss the Chief Wahoo logo controversy and the list of other ethnic mascots (Chef Boyardee, Aunt Jemima, Fightin' Irish).
jokes.punchline: 'You should have fought harder' — an outrageously provocative punchline that goes further than anyone in the audience expects.
jokes.explanation: An edgy joke that works structurally — the escalating list of 'logos' builds to a punchline that shocks. In 1998 terms this lands as provocative comedy; today it reads as more problematic than funny. Scored for its construction quality, not its ethics. The 'fought harder' line is genuinely ballsy for network (even HBO) television.

jokes.setup: Larry raises the 'women running the world = no war' platitude.
jokes.punchline: Carey's sarcastic dismissal of the cliché — implying women are just as capable of irrational conflict.
jokes.explanation: A competent anti-cliché joke but not particularly original. The setup is the real joke; Carey's sarcasm is the expected move.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Why don't we go out on that, 'cause then I can forward the letters right to you.'
jokes.setup: Carey has just made his controversial joke about women and war.
jokes.punchline: Larry's exit line — distancing himself by promising to forward the hate mail to Carey — delivered as a casual production decision.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Larry Sanders line — passive-aggressive, self-protective, wrapped in bland production talk. 'I can forward the letters right to you' is exactly how Larry deflects controversy. Excellent economy, strongly character-specific.

jokes.text: Post-segment: Carey tells Larry about a new Vegas bit: 'Great to be here at Caesars. I've only been here a day. I'm already up 10 grand. Of course, I had to let a fat Arab fuck me up the ass, but, hey.'
jokes.setup: Post-interview backstage, Carey pitches Larry a new bit for Vegas.
jokes.punchline: The Vegas 'up 10 grand' setup implies gambling success; the punchline reveals the actual means of earning it — violating multiple taboos simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: An aggressively transgressive joke designed to shock. The structure is solid (misdirection from gambling success to sexual transaction), but the reliance on ethnic slur and crudeness as the punchline feels more cheap than clever. Works in the context of a post-show backstage bit-pitching scene but not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: Backstage, Drew Carey to Larry: 'Yeah, but you mention one hooker, you gotta mention 'em all. You never think they could be so territorial, but Jesus Christ.'
jokes.setup: Larry says he wishes they'd talked more about Carey's personal life
jokes.punchline: Carey reveals there are multiple hookers who would need to be acknowledged — and they're territorial
jokes.explanation: The joke pivots from 'why didn't we talk about personal life' to an immediate, dark disclosure. The observation that hookers are 'territorial' is a funny, specific detail — it transforms the expected celebrity confession into something weirder. The economy is good and 'you mention one, you gotta mention 'em all' has a satisfying rhythm.

jokes.text: Larry learns the baby's father is one of tonight's guests. Carey asks about Larry's preference for women, then: 'Are you fucking my secretary?' Carey: 'No. You want me to?'
jokes.setup: Larry suddenly asks Carey (mid-flirtatious conversation about women) if he's sleeping with his secretary.
jokes.punchline: Carey's 'No. You want me to?' — an absurdly casual offer that completely wrong-foots the paranoid question.
jokes.explanation: The speed and casualness of 'No. You want me to?' is the joke — Carey turns a paranoid accusation into a light service offer. Well-structured and fast.

jokes.text: Staff backstage places their bets: 'I'll take Eriq La Salle. I'll take Michael Bolton.' — reducing the paternity situation to a sports-betting call.
jokes.setup: The betting pool continues as staff processes that it's not Drew Carey.
jokes.punchline: The casual finality of 'I'll take Bolton' — as if picking a fantasy team.
jokes.explanation: The running gag of treating Beverly's pregnancy as a betting event maintains its dark momentum. Functional.

jokes.text: Larry introduces Eriq La Salle's E.R. character arc: 'So tell me about how your character's coming along on E.R.' La Salle: 'Basically messed up and got his girlfriend pregnant, and they had a baby. Talk about human, right?'
jokes.setup: Larry asks about La Salle's character on E.R. — without yet knowing La Salle is Beverly's baby's father.
jokes.punchline: La Salle's character description exactly mirrors his real-life situation with Beverly — which neither he nor Larry consciously acknowledges on air.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best-constructed joke and a masterclass in dramatic irony. Larry unknowingly asks La Salle to describe his own real-life situation — 'messed up and got his girlfriend pregnant' — and La Salle delivers it straight ('Talk about human, right?'). The double meaning lands at maximum impact for an audience that knows both halves of the equation. This is exactly the kind of layered, earned comedy that defines the show at its best. The 'Talk about human, right?' closer is perfect.

jokes.text: Phil asks Beverly out to dinner. Beverly: 'I'm pregnant.' Phil: 'Hey, the more, the merrier.'
jokes.setup: Phil (oblivious or ignoring the pool) asks Beverly out to dinner on Larry's alleged recommendation.
jokes.punchline: 'Hey, the more, the merrier' — Phil's completely unfazed response to the pregnancy, reframing it as a bonus rather than a dealbreaker.
jokes.explanation: A short, perfectly economical joke. The setup is Beverly's pregnancy as a deterrent; the subversion is Phil's breezy enthusiasm. 'The more, the merrier' is highly quotable and the speed of the delivery (no hesitation, no horror) is what makes it land. One of the episode's most quotable moments.

jokes.setup: The betting pool narrows to Michael Bolton.
jokes.punchline: 'They're just a pair of lungs with a dick' — a magnificently crude dismissal of male pop singers.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable and economically excellent. 'A pair of lungs with a dick' is a great specific insult that generalizes beautifully. Works as the betting pool's natural conclusion and as a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Michael Bolton performs 'The Best of Love' while in the background Beverly and Eriq La Salle have their explosive confrontation about the pregnancy — cutting between the soppy love song and the actual drama.
jokes.setup: Bolton performs a heartfelt love ballad on stage while the human consequence of his bandmate's actions plays out in the wings.
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of 'the best of love' lyrics against Beverly confronting La Salle about an unwanted pregnancy he's trying to dodge.
jokes.explanation: A masterfully constructed set piece — the episode's longest sustained irony. The love song ('just keep givin' me the best of love') plays while the opposite is happening backstage. This is structural comedy at a high level: the show choreographs music and drama to maximize the ironic counterpoint. The fact that Bolton is innocent of the situation while providing the soundtrack makes it more absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: We should send bolton some flowers.

jokes.text: La Salle's response to Beverly telling him she's pregnant: 'Yes! Thank you!' — then immediately backpedaling.
jokes.setup: Beverly tells La Salle she's pregnant and that she called him four days ago.
jokes.punchline: La Salle's spontaneous 'Yes! Thank you!' — apparently a burst of genuine excitement — followed immediately by awkward backpedaling as he processes the situation.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully awkward reaction — La Salle's instinctive joy followed by conscious horror is a very human beat played for comedy. The 'whoa, whoa, whoa' that follows makes it land.

jokes.text: Beverly: 'I just told you I'm pregnant, and THIS is how you react? You're directing a film?' La Salle's attempt to spin his unavailability as being focused on 'doing the right thing' ends with Beverly: 'Let me help you out there. Just keep on doing what you've been doing — nothing.'
jokes.setup: La Salle tries to excuse his four-day non-response by saying he's been directing a film and 'trying to do the right thing.'
jokes.punchline: Beverly's devastating 'Let me help you out there. Just keep on doing what you've been doing — nothing.'
jokes.explanation: Beverly's 'nothing' is the perfect landing. The setup ('trying to do the right thing') invites a punchline and Beverly delivers it with precision: his 'right thing' is nothing. The build — 'let me help you out there' as a conversational setup to a devastating single word — is tight and earned.

jokes.text: Larry to Michael Bolton post-performance: 'My God, that was great, and I love the new haircut. It's fantastic.' Bolton: 'Still get the phantom tangle.'
jokes.setup: Bolton has cut his famous long hair. Larry compliments it.
jokes.punchline: 'Still get the phantom tangle' — Bolton's ghost-hair sensation, a play on phantom limb syndrome, delivered deadpan.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical three-word joke that reframes Bolton's famous hair loss as a medical condition. 'Phantom tangle' is a genuinely inventive coinage — the phantom limb analogy applied to hair is original and specific to Bolton in a way that makes it highly quotable. One of the best lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Larry learns from a staffer that Beverly's song on Bolton's album is 'The Best of Love' — the song Bolton just performed. Larry: 'You know, it's Beverly's favorite song on the whole album.' Bolton immediately understands and calls Larry 'a fucking asshole.'
jokes.setup: Larry casually mentions the song is Beverly's favorite — a seemingly innocent comment that Bolton reads as deliberate cruelty.
jokes.punchline: Bolton's explosion: 'You come in here, you knock up my assistant, and then you leave her, and then you come out here and sing.'
jokes.explanation: The payoff Larry's been building toward — but twisted. Larry confronts Bolton assuming he's the father, which he's not. Bolton's righteous fury is fully warranted but aimed at a misidentified target. The comedy of errors structure is smart, and 'you knock up my assistant, and then you come out here and sing' is a great line.

jokes.text: Bolton: 'First of all, I did not fuck your assistant. She's a fan of mine, she's been to a lot of shows, and I don't fuck all my fans, OK?'
jokes.setup: Larry has accused Bolton of impregnating Beverly.
jokes.punchline: Bolton's defense: 'I don't fuck ALL my fans' — implying he fucks some of them, which is its own revelation.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely funny denial that inadvertently confirms a worse truth. 'I don't fuck ALL my fans' is Bolton's defense, but the qualifier 'all' does a lot of work — suggesting that many fans are fair game. It's a perfect inadvertent self-incrimination joke with excellent economy.

jokes.text: After Bolton's denial, Larry pivots: 'That haircut is gay. Do you know that?' Bolton: 'Seriously? My haircut's gay?' Larry: 'No. Their haircut.' — gesturing at Bolton's band.
jokes.setup: The confrontation has hit an awkward moment after Bolton's denial. Larry suddenly pivots to commenting on the haircut.
jokes.punchline: When Bolton assumes Larry means his haircut, Larry redirects: 'No. Their haircut' — indicating the band.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured misdirection — Larry pivots from confrontation to hair critique as a deflection, and then when Bolton takes it personally, Larry further deflects to the band. The rhythm is perfect: the insult, the indignant response, the redirect. It's an unusual way to end a confrontation scene and very Larry Sanders — avoidance dressed as attack.

jokes.text: Larry: 'That haircut is gay. Do you know that?' Bolton: 'Seriously?' Larry: 'My haircut's gay?' Bolton: 'No. Their haircut.' Larry: 'Yes, it's your haircut, but you know, it goes with the, uh...'
jokes.setup: Larry, having just been humiliated in his accusation, pivots to attacking Bolton's appearance
jokes.punchline: Bolton questions whether Larry means his own haircut; Larry clarifies it's Bolton's, then trails off unable to complete his own insult
jokes.explanation: A wonderful cringe-comedy moment. Larry's retreat to a petty personal attack after his accusation failed is psychologically perfect. The confusion over whose haircut is gay, and Larry's inability to complete his own insult ('it goes with the, uh...') captures his crumbling social authority in real time. The stammering trail-off is Larry at his most human and most pathetic.

jokes.text: Bolton, preparing to leave after the haircut insult: 'I think it's time for me to go, OK?' Larry's goodbye: 'Hey, sensational, maestro. Come back real soon, will ya?' Bolton: 'Don't hold your breath.' Larry: 'You're terrific.'
jokes.setup: Bolton is angrily leaving after Larry accused him of paternity and insulted his band's hair.
jokes.punchline: Larry's reflexive show-host warmth ('Hey, sensational, maestro. Come back real soon') delivered to a man who just called him a fucking asshole — and Larry's final 'You're terrific' after Bolton says 'Don't hold your breath.'
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Larry Sanders: the performative show-host warmth kicking in automatically even after a personal confrontation. 'Sensational, maestro' and 'You're terrific' delivered to someone who just called him an asshole and said don't hold your breath is perfect character comedy. Only Larry Sanders would respond to 'Don't hold your breath' with 'You're terrific.' The character integration is exceptional.

jokes.text: Larry, post-Bolton: 'I feel better. I feel better. I think I put that guy in his place.' Staffer: 'Because it turns out it's La Salle.'
jokes.setup: Larry is self-congratulating on confronting (the wrong) Bolton.
jokes.punchline: The reveal: it was La Salle all along. Larry's triumphant confrontation was entirely misdirected.
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural payoff — and it's excellent. Larry's righteous indignation, his self-satisfaction ('I put that guy in his place'), and the entire Bolton confrontation was completely wrong. The reveal retroactively makes the La Salle E.R. irony (joke 43), Beverly's confrontation with La Salle, and Larry's oblivious questioning of La Salle all funnier. This is the kind of joke that works only because the rest of the episode has been building to it. 'We should send Bolton some flowers' is the perfect capper.

jokes.text: Final line: 'We should send Bolton some flowers.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just learned he wrongly accused Bolton of impregnating Beverly and verbally assaulted him.
jokes.punchline: 'We should send Bolton some flowers' — the pragmatic, show-biz response to having publicly humiliated an innocent guest.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the episode. Four words that encapsulate the show's entire worldview: the entertainment industry's reflexive, transactional response to human damage. 'Send him flowers' is both hilarious and a complete philosophy. It's the most economical joke in the episode and the one most likely to be quoted in isolation. The understatement is maximal — flowers for a false accusation of impregnating someone's assistant.
